title: The deathless path
hookLine: earnestness is the path to the deathless, heedlessness the path of death (Dhammapada 21)
tomorrow: should you ever point out someone else's faults?

lines: MISS A DAY AND IT'S GONE.
cards: An app streak runs on one small fear: miss a day and it's gone. The Dhammapada's second chapter makes a far bigger promise. Verse twenty-one calls earnestness the path to the deathless, and heedlessness the path of death.
Then it says the earnest do not die. And yesterday ended on the obvious problem. Everyone dies.
Earnest people too. So what is this verse actually saying?

teach.b: The puzzle gets solved at a deathbed. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha is old and ill. At Kusinara he lies down between two sala trees, and his monks gather close.
Three times he asks them: does anyone have a doubt about the teaching? Ask now. Silence each time.
Then his last words, in Rhys Davids's translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" And he dies. So the one who taught the verse died too.
The answer is in one Pali word.
Diligence in those last words is appamada, and it's the same word Max Müller translates earnestness in verse twenty-one: heedfulness, wakeful care.
The deathless, amata, is one of the names Buddhists give nibbana, the end of craving. So the verse never promised a body that lasts.
It says heedfulness is the path to the deathless, and that the heedless are like the dead even while they breathe. Buddhist teachers treat heedfulness as a daily practice, not a mood.
It's part of why, in Buddhist teaching, a slow walk, a meal or a broom can be a practice. And the Buddha's last sentence went to it, not to a farewell.
Earnest isn't grim. It's being awake to what you're doing, while you're doing it.

how: Buddhist teachers often name heedfulness (appamada) as the root of practice; in monasteries it is trained through ordinary tasks done with full attention, like walking, eating and sweeping.

o: heedful care that keeps you on the way to nibbana
a promise that good people live longer lives
trying so hard you never get tired or sick

games.q: the puzzle and its answer: tap the pairs.
p: the deathless, a name for nibbana
where the Buddha lay down at the end

s: verse 21 promises the earnest a body that won't die
the Buddha himself died; the deathless is nibbana.
the Buddha's last words use the same Pali word as verse 21
earnest here means serious and grim
it means heedful: awake to what you're doing, while you do it.

games.q: the Buddha lies between two sala trees, near the end. he asks if anyone has a last doubt. no one speaks. what are his last words?
o: a blessing on his monks, and a promise to come back to them.
decay is in all component things; work out your salvation with diligence.
a request that his monks build a great shrine to him.
games.why: he pointed them back to their own heedfulness: appamada, the same word as verse 21.

practice: Choose one small act within reach: pour a glass of water, fold one cloth, wash one cup. Do it as if it were the only thing today, every motion noticed, the weight, the sound, the stop.
Then sit with your hands still for whatever's left.

wordCard.voice: The deathless path: appamada, heedful care, which the Dhammapada calls the path to the deathless, to nibbana.

orig.note: Pali, written in Devanagari: heedfulness, earnestness; the word in verse 21 and in the Buddha's last words.

carryVoice: Keep this one: earnest, the word inside the Buddha's last sentence. Two steps into the verses.
